layout.title: A Full Checklist for Your Cooling Tower Quotation Evaluation

paragraphs: Cooling tower quotation evaluation should compare more than the purchase price.

Buyers should confirm that each vendor meets the same technical requirements, uses equivalent materials, includes commissioning support, and clearly defines what happens if the tower fails acceptance testing.
Many cooling tower buyers pick the lowest price and regret it later. Two quotes can look almost identical on paper, yet hide very different assumptions, materials, and service support.
The goal is to confirm that competing bids solve the same problem under the same conditions.
A low price often signals shortcuts you cannot see in a summary sheet. These shortcuts shift cost from the vendor to your plant over time.
Before you trust the cheapest number, check what that number leaves out. The most common hidden trade-offs include:
Every quote must start from the same design conditions. If vendors use different assumptions, the prices simply cannot be compared.
A standardized design basis is the foundation of a fair bid. Lock these inputs before you send the inquiry, and confirm that each vendor used them:
A tower designed for a lower wet-bulb temperature has an easier job than one designed for hot, humid site conditions.

If one vendor uses a lower wet-bulb value than the project requires, that quote may look attractive but may fail during actual operation. Buyers should confirm that every vendor uses the same design wet-bulb value.
Confirm each of these points appears in writing:
Performance curves show expected tower capability under different operating conditions. They help engineers compare vendors beyond the single design point.
Buyers should ask each vendor to include performance curves in the bid package.
CTI acceptance testing gives buyers a structured way to verify thermal performance.
For industrial projects, the contract should define who pays for the test, when the test occurs, which tolerance applies, and what remedy applies if the tower falls short.
Your material specification drives corrosion resistance, structural life, maintenance cost, and total ownership cost. Two quotes may claim the same capacity yet use very different material grades.
Before you accept any bid, confirm the exact grades and thicknesses. The items below most often hide cost-cutting:

Material selection should match the operating environment. Coastal sites may need stronger corrosion resistance. Chemical plants may need better resin and hardware selection. Seawater or dirty water applications may need different fill, nozzles, and basin protection.

High UV exposure, acidic air, high operating temperature, and poor water quality can all shorten service life when the material selection is weak. A thorough cooling tower quotation evaluation must account for these site-specific conditions to ensure the offered materials are up to the task.
Component selection affects performance, maintenance, energy use, and spare parts availability. The same tower size can carry very different internal quality.
A side-by-side component review protects long-term reliability. Compare these items across every bid:
Scope gaps create most hidden costs after purchase approval. A clear scope line protects both budget and schedule.
Each vendor should state, in writing, what is included and excluded. Confirm coverage for these items:
The detail here decides who pays for early failures.
Confirm each of these points:
Spare parts lead time can decide how fast a plant recovers from failure. A low-cost tower with long parts delays raises real downtime risk.
Ask about availability before you award the contract. Focus on the parts most likely to fail or wear:
A short list of direct questions exposes future supply risk. Ask each vendor:
When conducting a cooling tower quotation evaluation, look for realistic dates for engineering, manufacturing, shipping, installation, and commissioning. A timeline that ignores key steps will slip.
Review the full schedule, not just the delivery date. Confirm these milestones:
Payment terms should match project progress and risk. Heavy upfront payment shifts risk to the buyer.
Read the commercial section as carefully as the technical one. Confirm these terms:
Milestones link your cash to delivered value. They keep both sides accountable.
A performance bond protects the buyer if the vendor fails to meet contract obligations. It is most common on large industrial, EPC, or public-sector projects.
Review the bond as part of the commercial package. Confirm these details:

ICST supports your evaluation in practical ways:
Cooling tower quotation evaluation should compare technical and commercial terms together.

Spare parts lead time affects long-term reliability because unavailable parts can extend downtime. A performance bond and liquidated damages may protect large or high-risk projects. Buyers should compare vendors through a structured checklist and scorecard, not price alone.
It helps buyers compare bids fairly, identify hidden exclusions, reduce project risk, and choose the quotation that offers long-term value instead of the lowest upfront price.
It should use measurable values, not vague claims. Buyers should also ask for performance curves and acceptance testing terms before contract approval.

Material specification matters because materials affect corrosion resistance, service life, maintenance cost, and reliability. Buyers should check FRP grade, steel grade, basin material, fill media, fasteners, fans, drift eliminators, louvers, nozzles, coatings, and chemical resistance. Generic material descriptions can hide lower-quality substitutions that may fail early in harsh site conditions.
Be careful when coverage starts before commissioning or includes vague exclusions.

Spare parts lead time matters because long delays can extend downtime after a component failure. Buyers should ask about local stock, imported parts, emergency shipment, part numbers, and future support for fans, motors, gearboxes, nozzles, fill media, drift eliminators, bearings, drive shafts, sensors, and control components.

Lower-grade materials: A thinner gauge or cheaper resin cuts the price but shortens service life.
Excluded performance testing: No field test means no proof the tower meets its rated duty.
Unrealistic delivery: A short lead time may ignore drawing approval or shipping risk.
Hard-to-source spares: Long spare parts lead times can extend any future shutdown.
Scope gaps: Missing installation or commissioning becomes a paid change order later.
Heat load: The total heat the tower must reject.
Water flow rate: Confirm the same flow across all bids.
Hot water temperature: The inlet temperature to the tower.
Cold water temperature: The required outlet temperature.
Wet-bulb temperature: The single most important design input.
Range and approach: These define the tower’s real thermal work.
Site elevation and ambient conditions: These affect fan and capacity selection.
Water quality: Dirty or aggressive water changes fill and material choices.
Heat rejection duty: The total duty the tower must deliver.
Fan motor power and pumping head: These tie performance to energy use.
Drift and noise levels: Include these where the site requires limits.
Test code, tolerance, and timing: These define how and when you prove the result.
Remedy for shortfall: What the vendor must do if the tower fails the test.
Structural frame and FRP: Confirm grade, resin type, and load design.
Stainless and galvanized steel: Check the grade and the coating thickness.
Basin, fasteners, and hardware: Cheap hardware corrodes first and fast.
Fill media and drift eliminators: Check material, type, and thickness.
Louvers, fan blades, and fan stack: Confirm UV and weather resistance.
Nozzles and coatings: Check chemical resistance and the coating system.
Special suitability: Confirm seawater, dirty water, or acid resistance where relevant.
Fill media and drift eliminators: Match type to water quality and drift limits.
Fans, fan stacks, and motors: Compare efficiency, brand, and enclosure rating.
Gearboxes and drive shafts: Check serviceability and known reliability.
Nozzles and distribution headers: Confirm clog resistance and even flow.
Basin, louvers, and access platforms: Check design quality and maintenance access.
Vibration switches, controls, and VFDs: Confirm protection and control quality.
Engineering and structural design: Drawings and load calculations.
Tower, mechanical, and electrical supply: The core equipment package.
Controls and shipping: Including taxes, duties, and Incoterms.
Installation, erection, and commissioning: Who does the physical work.
Performance testing and training: Field test and operator handover.
O&M manuals and spare parts: Documentation and startup spares.
Site preparation and civil works: Foundations, piping, and wiring.
Crane and lifting support: Heavy lift responsibility on site.
Duration and start date: Confirm coverage starts at commissioning, not shipment.
Materials and workmanship: Coverage for defects in both.
Mechanical components: Fans, motors, gearboxes, and drives.
Exclusions: Note corrosion, water quality, and wear-part limits.
Claim process and response time: A clear, written path to resolution.
Labor and travel coverage: Confirm who pays for service visits.
Fill media and drift eliminators: Common wear and fouling items.
Fans, fan blades, and gearboxes: High-impact drivetrain parts.
Motors, drive shafts, and bearings: Long-lead items in some regions.
Couplings, louvers, and fasteners: Small parts that still cause delays.
Vibration switches, sensors, and controls: Critical for safe operation.
Which parts are stocked locally in Thailand or Asia?
Which parts are imported, and from where?
What is the average lead time for each?
Are parts interchangeable across models?
Are part drawings available?
Are emergency shipments possible, and how long will parts stay supported?
Drawing approval time: A real allowance for your review cycle.
Manufacturing lead time: Honest production duration.
Inspection and factory acceptance: Hold points where required.
Shipping and customs clearance: Especially for imported towers.
Installation and commissioning support: On-site vendor presence.
Performance testing window: Time set aside to prove the duty.
Currency, taxes, and freight terms: Know the true landed cost.
Payment milestones and advance payment: Tie payments to progress.
Performance bond and liquidated damages: Protect against vendor failure.
Validity, change order, and cancellation terms: Avoid surprise pricing later.
Dispute process: A clear path if disagreements arise.
Connect to progress: Tie payments to drawings, manufacturing, shipment, delivery, and commissioning.
Limit advance payment: Too much upfront raises buyer risk.
Bond amount and issuer: A credible bank or surety.
Validity and claim conditions: When and how you can call the bond.
Release conditions: What triggers the bond’s return.
Link to testing and completion: Tie the bond to acceptance and delivery.
Technical proposal review: Independent checks of vendor design and duty.
Cooling tower design and material review: Validation of selection and material specification.
Parts and component comparison: Side-by-side review of major components.
Performance testing support: Help with acceptance testing and validation.
Thermal upgrade and replacement planning: Guidance on lifecycle decisions.
Spare parts planning: Critical spares lists and supply planning.
Field support across Thailand and Asia: On-site maintenance and inspection help.
